MODULE 1 OF 6 · ABOUT 1.5 HOURS · BEGINNER

By the end of this module you will be able to

  • read a Lexis diagram and name the age, period and cohort direction of a cell;
  • build and inspect a rates object from the example data, a CSV file, or your own table;
  • combine cells (rates_chunk()), fill zero cells (rates_fill()) and interpolate ages (rates_i5());
  • draw a Lexis diagram with lexis_plot().

## The Lexis diagram {#the-lexis-diagram} ▶0:43Visualizing a Lexis diagramShort video made with the MATLAB toolbox ↗ A **Lexis diagram** is a grid with calendar **period** on one axis and **age** on the other. Each cell holds two numbers for a surveilled population: the **events** (for example, new cases of a disease, or deaths) and the **person-years** at risk. Their ratio is the **rate**, usually quoted per 100,000 person-years. Because everyone ages one year per calendar year, a person moves diagonally through the grid. All people in the same diagonal were born in the same years, so the diagonals are **birth cohorts**. For a cell with midpoints *a* (age) and *p* (period): $$\text{cohort} = p - a$$ A person aged 50 in 2000 belongs to the 1950 cohort. Every cell therefore carries all three time scales at once, and that is why APC analysis needs a model: age, period and cohort cannot be separated by reading the table. `lexis_plot()` shows the same rates twice: over age and period (left), and over age and birth cohort (right). Here it is for the first example dataset, with cells combined to 5 years of age by 5 years of period: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} R <- matisse_example(1) R55 <- rates_chunk(R, age_block = 5, per_block = 5) lexis_plot(R55) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Synthetic melanoma-like rates in women (example 1), 5 x 5 cells. Left: age by period. Right: the same cells by age and birth cohort.](m1-lexis-rates_files/figure-html/fig-lexis-1.png){#fig-lexis} ::: ::: Rates rise steeply with age, which dominates the picture. To see period and cohort effects you need a model that holds age fixed. That is the subject of [Module 2](m2-new-apc-model.qmd). ::: {.callout-note title="In the case studies"} The Europe study models 5-year age groups from 20 to 84 in 5-year periods (for example, 1973 to 2017 for England). It is a Lexis diagram of exactly this kind. :::
Hands-on lab20 min
## Rates objects {#rates-objects} In `matisseR`, a Lexis diagram is a **rates object**: a list whose two main parts are matrices with one row per age group and one column per period, `Events` and `Offset` (person-years). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} names(R) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Events" "Offset" "ages" "periods" "fullname" "event_label" [7] "description" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} dim(R$Events) # 50 single years of age x 29 calendar years ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 50 29 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} R$Events[1:3, 1:4] # the first cells: ages 35-37, years 1991-1994 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1991 1992 1993 1994 35 9 3 6 5 36 3 4 4 8 37 8 4 7 12 ``` ::: ::: `rates_uni()` gives a one-line summary, and `rates_long()` turns the matrices into a table with one row per cell, including the age, period and cohort midpoints: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rates_uni(R)[, .(ages, periods, cell, events, person_years, crude_rate)] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|ages |periods |cell | events| person_years| crude_rate| |:-----|:---------|:----|------:|------------:|----------:| |35-84 |1991-2019 |1x1 | 16339| 56075673| 29.1|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(rates_long(R), 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| age_lo| age_mid| per_lo| per_mid| events| offset| coh_mid| rate| |------:|-------:|------:|-------:|------:|------:|-------:|-------:| | 35| 35.5| 1991| 1991.5| 9| 44987| 1956| 20.0058| | 35| 35.5| 1992| 1992.5| 3| 46237| 1957| 6.4883| | 35| 35.5| 1993| 1993.5| 6| 47417| 1958| 12.6537|
::: ::: The `cell` column reads *age width x period width*: `1x1` means single years of age and single calendar years. ::: {.callout-tip title="Try it"} Open example 5 (breast cancer) and example 6 (lung cancer) with `matisse_example(5)` and `matisse_example(6)`. Compare their `crude_rate` in `rates_uni()`. Then draw `lexis_plot(rates_chunk(matisse_example(6), 5, 5))`. Where do you see the highest rates? :::
Reading + lab25 min
## Prepare rates for modelling {#prepare-rates-for-modelling} The APC model needs **square cells** (age and period intervals of equal width) and **no zero counts**, because it works on log rates. Three functions prepare a rates object. ### Combine cells with `rates_chunk()` `rates_chunk()` sums blocks of ages and periods. If the periods do not divide evenly, the leftover periods are dropped **from the start**, so the most recent data are kept: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} R55 <- rates_chunk(R, age_block = 5, per_block = 5) rates_uni(R55)[, .(ages, periods, cell, events)] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|ages |periods |cell | events| |:-----|:---------|:----|------:| |35-84 |1995-2019 |5x5 | 14716|
::: ::: The 29 single years from 1991 to 2019 became five 5-year periods, 1995-1999 to 2015-2019. The first four years (1991 to 1994) did not fill a block and were dropped. The total number of events fell accordingly. ### Fill zero cells with `rates_fill()` Small populations produce empty cells. Example 3 is a small population with many zeros: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} Z <- matisse_example(3) c(zero_cells_before = sum(Z$Events == 0), zero_cells_after = sum(rates_fill(Z)$Events == 0), fill_value = rates_fill(Z)$fill_value) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` zero_cells_before zero_cells_after fill_value 178.0 0.0 0.5 ``` ::: ::: `rates_fill()` replaces zero or missing counts with a small positive value (at least 0.5) so that log rates exist. If you have many zeros, combining cells with `rates_chunk()` first is usually better than filling. ### Interpolate ages with `rates_i5()` Registries often publish 5-year age groups. `rates_i5()` interpolates to single years of age; `"linear"` keeps the group totals, `"cubic"` gives smoother values: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} A5 <- rates_chunk(R, age_block = 5) # 5-year ages, single years of period I1 <- rates_i5(A5, "linear") c(age_groups_before = nrow(A5$Events), single_years_after = nrow(I1$Events), total_events_equal = sum(I1$Events) == sum(A5$Events)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` age_groups_before single_years_after total_events_equal 10 50 1 ``` ::: :::
Hands-on lab25 min
## Bring your own data {#bring-your-own-data} There are two common ways to get your data into a rates object. **From an NCI Age Period Cohort Web Tool file.** If you already prepared an input matrix for the [NCI web tool](https://analysistools.cancer.gov/apc/) (for example from SEER*Stat or the CI5 Plus database), read it directly with `csv2rates()`. The package's example files use this format: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} file <- system.file("extdata", "syn01_melanoma_F_A.csv", package = "matisseR") R_csv <- csv2rates(file) rates_uni(R_csv)[, .(object, ages, periods, cell, events)] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|object |ages |periods |cell | events| |:----------------------|:-----|:---------|:----|------:| |Synthetic melanoma F A |35-84 |1991-2019 |1x1 | 16339|
::: ::: Going the other way, `rates2csv(R, "my_rates.csv")` writes a rates object in the same format, so you can also run it in the web tool. **From a table of cases and person-years.** `rates_make()` takes a table with one row per age group and year: `age` (the 5-year group index, 1 = 0-4, 2 = 5-9, ..., 18 = 85+), `year`, `cases` and `py`. To practise, rebuild such a table from the example: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tab <- rates_long(R)[, .(age = floor(age_lo / 5) + 1, year = floor(per_lo), events, offset) ][, .(cases = sum(events), py = sum(offset)), by = .(age, year)] head(tab[order(age, year)], 3) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| age| year| cases| py| |---:|----:|-----:|------:| | 8| 1991| 37| 214518| | 8| 1992| 23| 220461| | 8| 1993| 31| 226555|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} R_make <- rates_make(tab, age_groups = 8:17, fullname = "Rebuilt from a table") # ages 35-39 to 80-84 rates_uni(R_make)[, .(ages, periods, cell)] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|ages |periods |cell | |:-----|:---------|:----| |35-84 |1991-2019 |5x1 |
::: ::: The cells are `5x1`: 5-year age groups but single calendar years. Combine periods to make them square: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rates_uni(rates_chunk(R_make, per_block = 5))[, .(ages, periods, cell)] ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|ages |periods |cell | |:-----|:---------|:----| |35-84 |1995-2019 |5x5 |
::: ::: ::: {.callout-important title="Check your own data before modelling"} Equal age and period widths, enough cases per cell (combine cells if many are empty), and consistent person-years across all cells. The [Resources](../resources.qmd) page links the slides on extracting SEER and CI5 Plus data. :::
Self-check5 min
## Self-check {#self-check} ::: {.quiz data-answer="2"} **A woman is aged 50 at the midpoint of the period 2000. Which birth cohort is she in?** 1. 2050 2. 1950 3. 1900 ::: explain Cohort = period - age = 2000 - 50 = 1950. The diagonals of a Lexis diagram are birth cohorts. ::: ::: ::: {.quiz data-answer="3"} **Why must zero counts be filled before you fit the APC model?** 1. Zeros make the Lexis diagram non-square. 2. The model needs person-years, not events. 3. The model works on log rates, and the log of zero does not exist. ::: explain The New APC model is fitted to log rates (by weighted least squares by default), so every cell needs a positive count. `rates_fill()` supplies a small positive value; combining cells with `rates_chunk()` first reduces the number of zeros. ::: ::: ::: {.quiz data-answer="1"} **You run `rates_chunk(R, age_block = 5, per_block = 5)` on 29 single calendar years (1991 to 2019). What remains?** 1. Five periods; the earliest four years (1991-1994) are dropped. 2. Six periods; the latest four years are dropped. 3. Five periods; the latest four years (2016-2019) are dropped. ::: explain 29 = 5 x 5 + 4. Leftover years are dropped from the start, so the most recent periods are kept: 1995-1999 up to 2015-2019. ::: :::
